title: One Outcome Per Hour
author: Workshop Bank
summary: Workshop Bank lays out a complete design method for facilitated sessions, arguing that most workshops fail not from lack of preparation but because the preparation is aimed at nothing in particular. The framework's core discipline is to give every hour one outcome, defined strictly as something participants will have created or decided and can hold, read or point to, rather than a theme like "explore team communication." It sets hard quotas (one outcome for an hour, two for a two-hour session, five or six for a full day) and recommends three scoping questions with the sponsor to surface which outcomes are worth the time. Each outcome is then built backwards into a roughly five-minute input, forty-minute working session and ten-minute share back, with the author insisting the share back is the last thing to cut because it is where people make sense of their work. Openings state outcomes and set the rule that participants talk while the facilitator runs the process; closings require named commitments with an owner and a check-in date within fourteen days. A worked half-day example on reopened decisions and broken handovers shows the whole design fitting on one page in about 45 minutes.
points: The test for a real outcome is finishing the sentence "By the end of this section, participants will have..." with a tangible artefact or decision, not a theme.
Outcome quotas (1 per hour, maximum 2 for two hours, 5 to 6 for a day) force clarity about what a session is for and give a principled answer to scope creep.
Each outcome gets a three-block hour: minimal input (about 5 minutes), a working session that produces the output (about 40), and a share back (about 10).
The share back should be protected because cutting it stacks input on input and makes earlier work evaporate.
Closings replace "any final thoughts?" with individual commitments that each carry an owner and a check-in date inside 14 days, and warm-ups survive only if they produce something.
quotes: I used to think the answer was more preparation. One more evening, a tighter deck and it would land. It never did.
This is where most designs go wrong. You sit down to plan and you write “explore team communication” or “improve how we make decisions.
A theme is what you point the room at. An outcome is what the room produces and takes away.
The quota forces you to decide what the session is for, and it gives you a straight answer when a client wants to bolt on three more.
But you’re only giving people enough to start working. Think of it as the briefing before a mission. If you’re still talking at six minutes, you’ve packed in more than the work needs.

But the share back is where people make sense of what they just did before the next thing lands on top of it. Cut it and you stack input on input, and by the end the first hour has evaporated. Protect it.

If your opening builds a bit of trust and gets a first thing onto paper, that is the first outcome. So keep the warm-up that feeds the session. Cut the warm-up that’s only there to fill the first ten minutes.

Give every hour one thing the room has to produce, and the design stops being a fight. You get there in about 45 minutes, on a single page, and every participant walks out holding something they made.
